point_of_view: Haspataal is the calm, quick colleague who has already thought of it.

principles.title: Have a point of view before a pixel
principles.instruction:
The founders of modernism designed with intent; the copies that followed kept the shapes and lost the reasons. A
generator gives you the most probable answer; without a point of view, that is all you get.

- Before designing a screen, write one sentence in its handbook page: who uses it, at what moment of their shift, and
  what "done" looks like for them (use the context of `get_ui_quality_brief`). A design without that sentence is not
  reviewed.
- Every departure from the design system's defaults names the pillar it serves: Calm, Quick, Thoughtful or Rooted.
- Feed the point of view to the generator: this guide, the screen's sentence and its context, never a bare "make a
  dashboard".

Ask: could this screen belong to any other product? If it could, it is not finished.

principles.title: Structure is the expression
principles.instruction:
Fazlur Rahman Khan's tube structures carried the tallest towers with the least material, and the structure itself
became the architecture. A bundle of tubes shared one core.

- One spine for every workspace: the same app shell, and a context bar that always shows **who** (the patient or the
  person acted on), **where** (the workspace, counter or ward) and **when** (the business date and the shift). The
  primary action sits in the same place on every screen.
- Every pixel of a working screen carries information or an action. Decoration lives only in the places D6 names.
- Density follows the job: at 100 % zoom on a 1366×768 display, front-desk and bench screens show the queue and the
  task together without scrolling. Review screens may breathe.
- The high-frequency task of each screen is reachable from its workspace home in at most two interactions, and by
  keyboard alone.

Ask: remove every colour and border; does the structure still read?

principles.title: Motion that carries load
principles.instruction:
Santiago Calatrava's structures move to do work: a roof opens to the sun, a bridge turns to let a ship through. Motion
is part of the structure, never applied to it.

- Animate only a change of state the user must notice: a bed turning Available, a token moving to the top, a discharge
  stage clearing, a result arriving.
- Budgets: 120-180 ms for a change of state, at most 240 ms for a navigation. No motion while the user types or scans,
  and none when the operating system asks for reduced motion.
- Never animate before the server confirms: no success movement for a write that has not committed (guide 16 Q3).
- Motion never delays input: the next keystroke or scan is accepted during any animation.

Ask: does this movement tell me something a still screen could not?

principles.title: Flow without seams
principles.instruction:
Zaha Hadid's spaces flow into one another; nothing stops at a hard corner.

- A patient's journey across roles (reception → doctor → laboratory → pharmacy → cashier; admission → ward →
  discharge) looks like one continuous place: the same identity block, the same status words and icons, the same colours
  for the same states in every workspace.
- No dead ends: every refusal says what to do next and offers it (the error's `details.next_step`, or the playbook's
  next call), and every completion offers the natural next task.
- Handovers are visible: a request waiting for someone else shows who, since when, and what happens next.

Ask: walk the journey end to end as each role; where did it feel like a different product?

principles.title: Rooted and humane
principles.instruction:
Frank Gehry builds for a place and its people, with warmth and with play.

- Urdu is an equal, not a translation layer: Noto Nastaliq Urdu set with its own line height, and right-to-left layouts
  designed and reviewed, never mirrored automatically.
- Words are the staff's words (token, slip, ward, counter, udhaar where staff use it), never internal codes.
- The signature motif is the **jaali**, the pierced screen of our architecture that keeps privacy and lets the light in.
  Use it as a quiet texture on the login, the workspace launcher, empty states and the help, never behind patient
  data, money or tables.
- Care shows in the details people meet every day: the business date and the shift in the header (as a calendar icon
  that shows today's date), the counter's name on the slip, a greeting by name at login, a token number large enough to
  read across a waiting hall.

Ask: would a receptionist in Lahore or Multan feel this was made for them?

principles.title: Calm by default, loud by exception
principles.instruction:
- Character lives in empty states, first runs and help, completions, idle and login screens. It never appears in
  clinical alerts, refusals about patients or money, or error messages.
- Alerts follow the backend's presentation (open decision H10): Code Red interrupts; everything else updates the screen
  and, at most, shows a dismissible notice. Character never softens or delays an alert.
- Colour is never the only signal (guide 16 Q4). The jaali and the brand colours never resemble a status colour.

Ask: in a busy hour, is anything on this screen shouting that should not be?

principles.title: Speed is the first delight
principles.instruction:
- A keystroke, click or scan shows its effect within 100 ms. A workspace opens with its data within 1 second on the
  hospital LAN. The lists of a working day scroll without visible stutter.
- Every high-frequency task has a keyboard path and works with a barcode scanner, without the mouse.
- Decorative motion and textures switch off while the user works in a rapid loop (three or more submissions or scans
  within ten seconds) and return when they pause.
- The busiest-hour test: an experienced user completes the screen's main task twenty times in a row with fresh data.
  Record the median and the slowest times. No character element may be in the slowest path.

Ask: did anything beautiful cost a second?

principles.title: Encode the standard into the system
principles.instruction:
Gutenberg cast far more pieces of type than the alphabet needs, so that machine-set pages looked hand-made: his system
was both extensible and opinionated. When building is spread across many hands and agents, the object of design is
no longer the screen; it is the system.

- The design system the frontend lead owns (H09) encodes these principles as tokens (the motion budgets, the jaali
  motif, type scales for both scripts, density levels). It also provides complete templates and flows, not only
  components: the patient-identity pattern, a validated write, a pending approval, a correction, a print.
- Each component has the variants a hospital needs: dense and comfortable, English and Urdu, 100 % to 250 % zoom,
  Light and DarkHighContrast.
- A new screen starts from a template and its flow; a deviation is recorded with its reason (guide 16 Q2).

Ask: if three agents built this screen from the same prompt, would they produce the same product?

principles.title: Done is not good: the editor
principles.instruction:
Anything can now be built in a week. The filtering that used to happen before building must happen after it, and
someone must own it.

- A named editor (the frontend lead or someone they appoint, never the screen's author) reviews every workspace end to
  end as its users would, after guide 17's review and in addition to it.
- The editor's pass goes one level deeper than the user will consciously see: alignment and spacing, Urdu line breaks,
  the state between two states, the order focus moves in, the wording of every message.
- The editor records at least three iterations (before and after screenshots, and what changed) for each of the ten
  busiest screens: registration, the doctor's queue and consultation, the pharmacy counter, the laboratory bench, the
  bed matrix, the admissions desk, the cashier's shift, the ward's beds and medication chart, the approvals queue and
  the workspace launcher.
- A system can satisfy every rule and still be dead (Christopher Alexander). The editor may send back a screen that
  passes every check but has no life, with the reason.

Ask: what would make a user say "they thought of that"?

principles.title: Protect the strange
principles.instruction:
Generic patterns are safe and forgettable. The tools that make building cheap also make it cheap to try something
better; spend some of that saving on making something unmistakably ours.

- The frontend team develops three signature interactions where Haspataal should feel unlike generic software, each
  held to D7's budgets:
  1. the bed matrix as a plan of the building: wards read like floors at a glance, not a grid of rows;
  2. the queue as a token hall: large numerals, the next patient called with a calm movement, readable across the room;
  3. the discharge as a path of stages: the patient moves along it, and the stage holding them is unmistakable.
- Improve the inputs, then stress the outputs: give the generator this guide, the screen's sentence, the brand words and
  real examples of the place; then have the result critiqued by another agent and judged by the editor before it ships.
- Give designers room to explore: a deviation in a signature interaction is welcome when it is better for the user and
  passes D7.

Ask: what here could only be Haspataal?

zombie_ui_checklist: It could be any product: generic cards, generic icons, stock illustrations, placeholder text.
The same dashboard layout is reused for roles with different jobs.
A spinner without words, or a blank screen, while data loads.
A status shown by colour alone, or one colour used for two meanings.
A success message before the server confirmed it.
A dialog on top of a dialog, or a dead end with no next step.
Decoration in a working table, a form or an alert.
Urdu laid out by mirroring the English screen without review.
Motion longer than its budget, or motion while the user types or scans.

context.title: General consent at admission
context.purpose: The general consent of every admission (the need, the estimated stay and cost, the hospital rules), printed in the patient's language, signed and scanned.

rubric.label: Design principles applied
rubric.hint: The screen meets guide 18 (D1-D10) and none of its zombie-UI checklist: the one-sentence brief is in its handbook page, its motion keeps the budgets, Urdu is laid out on its own, and the busiest-hour test is recorded (D7).

rubric.label: Editor's pass
rubric.hint: A named editor other than the screen's author reviewed the workspace end to end as its users would (guide 18 D9), with the iterations recorded for the busiest screens.

use: Write the screen's one-sentence brief (D1) first; design within these principles and guide 16; an editor other than the author reviews the workspace (D9).
